note_tweet.text:
Shared Meta Muse pages could be found by people who were never sent the link

Muse is Meta's AI assistant, launched in the US on September 8. When a user asks it to share something, Muse makes a web page that anyone with the link can open without logging in. Security firm Claroc says Muse built each page's web address from the title of what was shared plus a random code, so a made up example would start with "home-sale-budget".

Every time a browser opens a web address, it looks the name up in the internet's address book, called DNS, and commercial services keep searchable logs of those lookups. Claroc says one search of such a service returned more than 6,800 Muse addresses, readable by title. Its researchers opened a few hundred without an account and found a small business owner's loan application, a marketing company's revenue review marked for its CEO, and a job candidate's notes for a confidential call with an AI lab. Claroc says it has no evidence anyone misused the pages, but it cannot tell whether anyone else found them first.

Claroc says it reported the problem to Meta's bug bounty program on October 8 and published its research on October 18. Meta told Ars Technica on October 20 that it had paused sharing. On October 22, Meta's David Singleton wrote on X that "the underlying issue is now fixed" and that items shared before the fix now have new addresses. He says the flaw affected shared "artifacts," such as documents and images made in Muse, and not chat sharing. Meta has not said how the new addresses are built, and Claroc's report, last updated October 20, does not say whether it has tested the fix. Claroc says the old addresses, titles included, are still in those lookup logs, out of Meta's reach.

The Sesame Disk post explains how a share link can be built so its address gives nothing away. From the post: "Put the secret in the path, never in the hostname."

Read the full post: https://t.co/EE34rsuIs5

Sources: [Claroc](https://t.co/6almmsRATt), [Ars Technica](https://t.co/MhkUMe4ioz), [The Verge](https://t.co/09AJDoiKP7) and [David Singleton on X](https://t.co/xop63AmBXl).
